section.title: Chapter review and projects
section.p: Chapter 16 started with infinite polynomials and ended with a warning about their limits. The main thread was approximation with control.

A power series is a function-building machine. A Taylor polynomial is a finite local approximation. A Taylor series is what happens when the degree grows without bound. Taylor’s theorem tells us when the finite approximations actually approach the function.

exercise.title: What is the difference between a Taylor polynomial and a Taylor series?

statement.p: A Taylor polynomial is a finite local approximation with a remainder. A Taylor series is the infinite limit of those polynomials. In your own words, why does \lim T_n(x)=f(x) not follow from the mere fact that T_n is the Taylor polynomial of f?

hint.p: Matching derivatives at a point produces the polynomials. Equality with the function is a statement about leftovers tending to zero, which can fail even if the series converges.

exercise.title: Why does a series calculator need a stopping rule?

statement.p: A sine calculator built from Taylor polynomials is an algorithm only when it knows when to stop. In your own words, why is a list of more and more terms not yet a computation, and what does an error bound add that a graph of partial sums cannot replace?

hint.p: An algorithm must guarantee a tolerance, not merely look as if it has settled. Remainder estimates convert an infinite process into a finite, checkable procedure.

exercise.title: What three questions should every power series answer?

statement.p: The review asks, every time: what is the center, where does the series converge, and if it is a Taylor series, why does it equal the function? In your own words, why are those three questions a complete checklist rather than optional extras?

hint.p: Center locates the local data. Convergence names the domain. Remainder vanishing is the only bridge from the formal series back to the original function.

exercise.title: What do the sine and cosine series hide together?

statement.p: The series for e^x, \sin x, and \cos x are now in hand, and they will produce Euler’s formula. In your own words, why is it plausible that those three series belong to one rotating picture rather than three unrelated identities?

hint.p: Sine and cosine are the even and odd pieces of a single exponential series after the substitution that turns powers into a cycle of signs. The next chapter makes that cycle into a direction in the plane.
